_note: How each surface finish is previewed in Blender.
Keyed on the readable finish label, not the raw index: the index is only
meaningful inside its own material group - index 1 is 'Inverted Gloss
Finish' on a corvette palette and plain 'Rust' on a legacy one. These
labels come straight from DT_Palettes.csv, which is also what the colour
picker shows, so what you pick in the UI is what is looked up here.
THE VALUES ARE OURS, NOT THE GAME'S. What No Man's Sky actually does to
its shader per finish was never worked out - the extracted
material_finishes.json carries names and indices and nothing else - so
these are chosen to tell the finishes apart in the direction their names
point. Tune them here; nothing else reads them, and none of it touches
the saved UserData, so the game stays the authority on how a base really
looks. This only changes what Blender draws.
Fields, all optional - an absent one means 'leave it alone', and a label
absent from this file renders exactly as its textures make it:
polish     how much of the part's own roughness to TAKE AWAY, 0..1.
The library drives roughness from (1 - MASKS.red) and those
maps are rough - the median texel sits between 0.38 and 0.78
across the trims - so an offset alone can only ever make a
part rougher. This is the field that makes a gloss glossy:
final = texture * (1 - polish) + roughness. 0 keeps all of
the texture's roughness, 1 removes all of it.
roughness  ADDED to the part's own roughness map, clamped to 0..1.
It is an offset, NOT the roughness. "roughness": 1 does
not mean 'roughness of 1', it means 'add 1 to whatever the
map says', which pins the part at fully rough no matter
what else is set. Use small values - 0.15 to 0.40 - to make
a part ROUGHER, and use polish to make it smoother. The
same goes for metallic.
metallic   added to the part's own metallic map, clamped to 0..1.
The green channel of MASKS is ALREADY a good metal mask -
31-87% of texels read as metal across the trims - so a large
offset here does not make a part metal, it flattens the mask
and makes every painted and cloth area metal too. Metal that
does not look like metal is nearly always a roughness
problem, not a metallic one: pair a small offset with a high
polish. Metallic also kills the diffuse term, so a value
that lands near 1 everywhere turns the part into a dark
mirror and the palette colour stops reading at all.
tint       This is the ONLY field that can make a part look rusty,
dirty or weathered. Roughness and polish change how shiny a
surface is and nothing else - no amount of roughness will
ever read as rust, because rust is a colour. A tint that is
close to grey barely shows at all: it has to be an actual
oxide colour to read as one.
[r, g, b] MULTIPLIED over the part, so it is brighter than
the colour you want out: a rust of [0.55, 0.26, 0.14] lands
as dark oxide over a light hull. Multiply rather than mix so
the panel lines, decals and paint survive underneath.
tint_mix   how strongly, 0..1. 0 is no tint at all.
invert     true swaps the palette slots, p<->s and t<->q.
COLOUR MUST SURVIVE THE FINISH. 'invert' and a heavy 'tint' change the
colour the part was built with, which is the one thing a finish must not
do casually. Only the finish the game itself calls 'Inverted' should
carry invert. The four 'Legacy - *' finishes cover all 16 LEGACY palettes
and so almost every classic base - they are roughness only on purpose,
and anything that inverts or tints them reads as 'the colours are wrong'
across the whole build.
Keys starting with _ are notes like this one and are ignored.
Saving this file is enough - the table re-reads itself when the file
changes on disk. The new values reach a part the next time it is
recoloured, so recolour (or re-place) the part to see an edit.
